original_question: Characterize which achievement sets in R^2 are homeomorphic to each other; equivalently, classify planar achievement sets up to homeomorphism.
target_in_paper: Section 5, Problem 25: "Characterize achievement sets in R^2 up to homeomorphism."
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's intended target almost verbatim: it stays in the planar setting R^2, asks for a classification by homeomorphism type, and does not drift to a neighboring problem about cuts, sections, interiors, or special families such as geometric pairs (p^n,q^n).
missing_details: The draft should explicitly define a planar achievement set: for an absolutely convergent series sum_{n=1}^infty (x_n,y_n) in R^2, E((x_n,y_n)) := { sum_{n=1}^infty epsilon_n (x_n,y_n) : epsilon_n in {0,1} for all n }.

It should state the quantifier scope: the classification ranges over all absolutely convergent vector series in R^2, not arbitrary subsets of R^2 and not higher-dimensional Banach-space achievement sets.
It should make explicit that the task is to determine the homeomorphism classes realized by such sets, equivalently to decide when two sets of the form E((x_n,y_n)) are homeomorphic.
For stand-alone clarity, it helps to note that these are compact subsets of R^2, since they arise from absolutely convergent series.

The nearby context shows that the problem is not just to sort among the nine elementary planar types listed in Proposition 3.1 of [35]; the paragraph after Problem 25 notes that Theorem 4.1 of [35] yields at least one further topological type via horizontal sections by sets of P-sums.
refined_question: Characterize, up to homeomorphism, the subsets of R^2 that arise as planar achievement sets of absolutely convergent series; that is, determine exactly which homeomorphism classes are realized by sets of the form E((x_n,y_n)) := { sum_{n=1}^infty epsilon_n (x_n,y_n) : epsilon_n in {0,1} for every n }, where sum_{n=1}^infty (x_n,y_n) is an absolutely convergent series in R^2.
justification: This is the exact open problem stated in Section 5 as Problem 25. The only paper-critical additions needed to make your draft fully stand-alone are the definition of a planar achievement set and the absolute-convergence hypothesis on the generating series. The same nearby paragraph explains that the problem is a genuinely global homeomorphism-classification problem for planar achievement sets, not merely a classification among the nine elementary types already exhibited in the earlier paper [35], because the survey explicitly notes that [35, Theorem 4.1] forces at least one additional topological type.
